chapter_theme: In the last ilampakam the teacher continues to show the king the sufferings of hell, of animals and of men, naming the sins that lead to them, so that the king turns from pleasure and kingship toward renunciation.

cast.role: the teacher preaching the dharma to Civakan in the last ilampakam
the hero, now an old king, who is addressed

2774.reading: The teacher begins the tortures of hell: sinners are plunged in molten copper, set on a machine swing to be burnt, ground in an oil-press and pounded to powder, so that a pain heavy as a mountain is their daily labour.
2774.nuance: The verse names no sin; the cause comes in the verses that follow (2776 and after).
2774.event: The teacher describes the daily tortures of the hell-dwellers.

claims.claim: those who have done evil suffer endless bodily torture in hell each day

2775.reading: The teacher asks who goes into the hell where men, strengthless as ploughing oxen, fall in rich mire and sink under thick smoke, and tells the king to listen.
2775.event: The teacher turns from the hell's tortures to ask who is sent there, and bids the king listen.

2776.reading: Those who are bent only on killing, the cruel and hard-hearted, and those who say there is no other world and no soul, and that penance and giving are a loss, go into hell borne in the cars of their evil deeds.
2776.nuance: The denial of this world's other and of the soul is put in the mouth of those the verse sends to hell, so the work answers it here by its consequence, not by argument; the account of the deniers is the teacher's, not their own.
2776.event: The teacher names the killers and the deniers of the next world as the ones who go to hell.

claims.claim: killing beings sends the doer to hell
there is no next world or soul, and penance and giving are a waste

2777.reading: The verse turns to the pains of hell and of animals, saying hell is of the nature of fire and water and that animals have pains of their own, and calls the king the lord of the spear and the flowery garland.
2777.nuance: The wording of lines 1 to 3 is dense and rests on a repeated -நீரவே, so the exact comparison is uncertain.
2777.event: The teacher compares the suffering of hell with that of animals.

2778.reading: The teacher says the sufferings animals bear, as deer cry out on the cloud-touching hill when the strong beast roars, are what a king who never tires of desire will also undergo.
2778.nuance: Line 4 turns on வேந்து உறூஉம் துன்பம், which can mean either that kings suffer like the deer or that kings cause such suffering; I take the first.
2778.event: The teacher compares the fear of deer before the lion with the suffering a king incurs.

claims.claim: a king's pleasures bring him pain like that of hunted beasts

2779.reading: Hounds with dripping mouths and fiery eyes, cruel as Death, are let loose, and flocks of peacocks hide their necks in fear.
2779.event: Hunters set dogs on peacocks, which cower and hide their necks.

2780.reading: The teacher scorns those who smear a lamb with turmeric, garland it, cut its throat and sprinkle its blood, and say that the gods enjoy this; he says that in Yama's world this is repaid fourfold.
2780.nuance: The view that gods delight in the offered blood is set in order to be answered in line 4 by the recompense in Yama's world; the speaker's account of it is that of a critic. நான்மடங்கு may mean fourfold or the fourth part, so the measure is uncertain.
2780.event: Worshippers slaughter a goat for the gods; the teacher tells the king what awaits them.

claims.claim: the gods are pleased by the blood of a slaughtered animal

2781.reading: Women's relish for roasted meat means a pregnant monitor lizard, a red-eyed carp and a young fish are each cut up separately, and the teacher asks whose eyes would not look on the creature that gapes and wails.
2781.nuance: The verse asks the king to see the wound as the animal's own, which is the very appeal of Kural 257.
2781.event: Animals are butchered and roasted to be eaten.

2782.reading: Sea, forest, stomach and hill are no refuge: when pain tortures a creature it can find no shelter and perishes in grief.
2782.event: Animals in pain find that no place shelters them.

claims.claim: in suffering a being has no protector in the sea, forest or hills

2783.reading: Plough-oxen are driven and beaten by the wicked until they die; crows eat them where no one drives them off, and the worms come out of them in their unbearable pain.
2783.event: Cruel men beat the plough-ox to death, and crows feed on it.

2784.reading: Pack-oxen sink in the sand of a half-dry river carrying their loads like the great merchants, press their sides and noses to the ground, and die, their bodies rotting, without grazing.
2784.event: Burden-bearing oxen die in the river sand.

2785.reading: Young bull elephants torn by sharp iron, pierced by spears, trumpeting like rain-clouds and grieving for their cow elephants, roam and are consumed by fever.
2785.event: Elephants are hunted with iron and spears.

2786.reading: The hunters smoke the elephant into giving up life for the sake of tusk, hair and pearl, and the teacher addresses the king as the one whose chest wears Fortune.
2786.nuance: Line 2 is hard to read in places (மாலிபோல் நீராம்), so the exact picture of the hunt is uncertain.
2786.event: Hunters kill elephants with fire and smoke for their tusks and pearls.

2787.reading: Animals are made to lie down at the sacrificial fire, at the sword's edge, and in the long net, and the teacher says that those not kin to us are all worn out in this way.
2787.nuance: The verse mentions sacrifice (வேள்வி) among the killings but does not argue against it; that is done in 2780.
2787.event: Animals are slain in sacrifice, by the sword and in nets.

2788.reading: Killers, those who pen birds in cages, and men who are not hunters either, the green parrots and mynas parted from their kin: all of them cause pain.
2788.event: Men cage birds and separate them from their kin.

claims.claim: separating creatures from their kin and caging them causes suffering

2789.reading: Those who revile the great ascetics, sinners who do not share their food, and courtesans who sell themselves are told they will be born as animals.
2789.nuance: Line 2 reads பகுட்ததுணா for பகுத்துண்ணா, which I take as 'who do not share their food'.
2789.event: The teacher names the sins whose fruit is rebirth as an animal.

claims.claim: reviling ascetics, hoarding food and selling the body lead to rebirth as an animal

2790.reading: Turning from animals, the teacher tells the king he will now hear the fierce pains of men who gaze on their own shadows, sink in pleasure, and play with young women's shoulders.
2790.event: The teacher begins the account of human suffering.

claims.claim: those who live for pleasure will suffer grave pain

2791.reading: Wrapped in the two membranes of the womb, enclosed in a skin of filth swarming with worms, wearing foul entrails, those who have come into the wilderness of birth should be thought of.
2791.nuance: The grammar of lines 3 and 4 is hard, but the picture of the body as a bag of filth is clear; the reading of the wilderness as birth is mine.
2791.event: The teacher describes the suffering of the body in the womb and birth.

2792.reading: Men are impaled and sawn for their passion for women, trampled by a mad elephant, and die in the sea of sorrow.
2792.event: The teacher lists the punishments that befall lovers of women.

claims.claim: passion for women leads to punishment and death in a sea of sorrow

2793.reading: The sea-going ship that heaves like a bull elephant capsizes in the wind; the teacher tells the king that what people suffer is a fourth step of hell.
2793.nuance: நான்காம் அடி is obscure; I take it to say that the pains of this world are one fourth of hell's.
2793.event: The teacher describes a ship capsizing and says human suffering is part of hell's.

2794.reading: Householders who bear the yoke of duty are choked by smoke, stand in the mire, are struck, and are worn out when their hands are bound before they can say their wrong.
2794.nuance: The verse sets household wealth against renunciation, the opposite of Kural 46's argument.
2794.event: The teacher describes the suffering of householders under the yoke.

claims.claim: the householder's wealth and duty are a yoke of suffering

2795.reading: Eyes gouged out, hands and feet cut off, flesh broken by blows, and the wounds worked on with elbows are the pains of the punished.
2795.nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are obscure in places.
2795.event: The teacher describes the punishments given to criminals.

2796.reading: For kings with the garlanded umbrella, taking the world is pain, guarding it is greater pain, and without a woman's embrace the sorrow grows like the sea.
2796.event: The teacher says kingship is suffering.

claims.claim: the king's conquest and protection of the world bring great sorrow

2797.reading: The body is a tall grove of flesh; sickness is a red fire that lodges in it, beauty its flowers withered, and it burns and dies.
2797.event: The teacher says the body burns and dies like a grove on fire.

claims.claim: the body is perishable and consumed by disease

2798.reading: The bent back, the shaking, the old age that falls like a ripe fruit, and the other diseases are pains that cannot be fully told.
2798.nuance: Line 1 compares the bent back to an elephant's pulled, bent form; the exact comparison is unclear.
2798.event: The teacher closes the account of suffering with old age and disease.

links.note: 2774 gives hell's tortures by molten copper and the oil-press without a cause; Tirumanthiram 198 binds those who urged 'kill, stab' and sets them in fire-mouthed hell.
links.teaches: Together they show hell as the fruit of a named sin and as a daily mechanical punishment, which neither shows alone.

gains.a: the verse names no crime for its tortures, and gains the sin of urging killing
gains.b: 198 gives only a fiery pit, and gains the machines and repeated daily torment

links.note: 253 names killing and eating flesh among the sins that sink into leprosy and hell; 2776 names the killers and the deniers of the next world as those who go.
links.teaches: The reader sees the Cintamani widen the list of sinners from conduct (253) to belief, since the one who denies the next world is sent there too.

links.note: 2776 sends those bent on killing into hell on the cars of their sins; Kural 321 says killing brings all other evil deeds with it.
links.teaches: The couplet states killing as the root of other wrongs, and the epic adds the journey to hell as its end.

gains.a: the verse gains a rule naming killing as the first of all sins, which it presupposes
gains.b: the couplet gains a picture of where such deeds lead, which it leaves unsaid

links.note: 2780 attacks the sacrifice of a lamb for the gods' pleasure with the recompense in Yama's world; Kural 259 weighs a thousand oblations against not killing and eating one creature.
links.teaches: The epic condemns the sacrificer by his punishment while the Kural condemns by comparison of worth, so the reader sees two ways to refuse sacrifice.

gains.a: the verse gains a measure of worth for sacrifice set against not killing
gains.b: the couplet gains a consequence after death and a scene of blood, which it lacks

links.note: 2781 asks whose eyes would look on the creature cut apart and wailing; Kural 257 says flesh would not be eaten by those who saw it as another's wound.
links.teaches: The epic stages the very seeing that the couplet only wishes for, and shows it fails when appetite rules.

gains.a: the verse gains a name for what is being asked, seeing flesh as a wound
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene of the wounded animal, where it states only a condition

links.note: 2789 sends those who revile ascetics and the sinful to animal birth; 943 tells a dog that, leaving its dog's body, it will gain a god's body through the mantra.
links.teaches: The same Cintamani shows rebirth moving down by sin and up by holy words, so an animal body is not final.

links.note: 2791 shows the body as a skin of filth swarming with worms; Siddhar 41 calls it a worm-nest from which excrement and urine flow.
links.teaches: Both teach disgust at the body, one to warn of birth, the other to leave the body for the feet of Siva.

gains.a: the verse gains a goal beyond disgust, which the Siddhar names as the feet
gains.b: the Siddhar song gains the womb and birth as the origin of the body's filth

links.note: 2794 says the householders' wealth is a yoke of toil and pain; Kural 46 asks what one gains by going outside the household life if it is lived by dharma.
links.teaches: Whether household life is a yoke or the best path depends on the claim of 2794, and the two works cannot both hold it.

gains.a: the verse gains the Kural's own defence of the householder, which it argues against
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-view that names the householder's wealth as the pain

links.note: 2796 says taking and guarding the earth is pain for kings; 27 says Civakan, fearing kingship like a snake struck by thunder, renounces after hearing dharma.
links.teaches: The hero's renunciation is the answer to this teaching, so the reader sees what the teacher's argument was meant to do to him.

links.note: 2797 says the body is a grove burned by the fire of disease; Siddhar 63 says this life has no standing, like a bubble on water.
links.teaches: Jain teacher and Siddhar agree that the body does not stand, but one asks escape from disease and the other from rebirth by grace.

gains.a: the verse gains a prayer for release, which the Siddhar adds
gains.b: the Siddhar song gains a concrete picture of how the body ends, in disease

source_issues: Verses 2774-2776, 2778, 2785 and 2787 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2789 line 2 reads பகுட்ததுணா, apparently for பகுத்துண்ணா.
